textos.2aea05fc-aacb-42f9-9652-21fe581c46ed#309: Each form or set of forms includes a data environment. The data environment is an object that includes the tables or views that the form interacts with and the relationships between tables that the form expects. You can use the data environment to automate opening and closing tables and views when the form is run. In addition, you can use the data environment to set the ControlSource Property property for controls by populating the ControlSource property in the Properties Window ([[T0]]) with all the fields in your data environment.

You can visually design the data environment and save it with the form. When you add tables or views to the Data Environment designer, you can see the fields and indexes that belong to the table or view.

- Open the form in the Form Designer .
- On the View menu, click Data Environment . The Data Environment designer opens for the form's data environment.
- On the DataEnvironment menu, click Add .
- In the Add Table or View dialog box, click the database you want in the Database list.
- In the Select area, click Tables or Views .
- In the Tables in database list, click the table or view you want to add to the data environment.
- Click Add . Tip If no database or project is open, click Other to browse for and select a table.

You can also drag a table or view from an open project or the Database Designer ([[T0]]) to the Data Environment designer.

The following list includes commonly set data environment properties:
 - AutoCloseTables Property
- AutoOpenTables Property
- InitialSelectedAlias Property
You can set the order your records appear in your report by setting an index for the data environment.

- From the View menu, choose Data Environment .
- From the shortcut menu, choose Properties .
- In the Properties Window, choose Cursor1 in the Object box.
- Choose the Data tab and select the Order property.
- Enter an index name. - [[T0]] - Select an index from the list of available indexes.

When the Data Environment Designer is active, the Properties Window ([[T1]]) displays objects and properties associated with the data environment. Each table or view in the data environment, each relationship between tables, and the data environment itself is a separate object in the Object box of the Properties window.
When you remove a table from the data environment, any relationships that the table is involved in are also removed.

- In the Data Environment Designer , select the table or view.
- From the DataEnvironment menu, choose Remove .

If you add tables to the Data Environment Designer that have persistent relationships set in a database, the relationships are automatically added in the data environment. If the tables don't have persistent relationships, you can still relate them in the Data Environment Designer.

- Drag a field from the primary table onto the matching index tag in the related table.

You can also drag a field from the primary table to a field in the related table. If there is no index tag in the related table corresponding to the field in the primary table, you're prompted to create the index tag.

The RelationalExpr Property property is set by default to the name of the primary key field in the primary table. If the related table is indexed on an expression, you need to set the RelationalExpr property to this expression. For example, if the related table is indexed on [[I0]], you need to set RelationalExpr to [[I1]].

If the relation is not a one-to-many relationship, set the OneToMany Property property to false ([[T2]]). This corresponds to using the [[T3]] Command command without issuing [[T4]] Command.

Setting the OneToMany property of a relation to true ([[T5]]) corresponds to issuing the [[T6]] command. When you skip through the parent table, the record pointer remains on the same parent record until the record pointer moves through all related records in the child table.

> **Note:** If you want a one-to-many relationship in the form, set the OneToMany property to true ([[T7]]), even if a persistent one-to-many relationship has been established in a database.

textos.2b5b18e4-b902-4d8a-8cb7-4eef9f3a60a3#314:
Included for backward compatibility. Use the CommandButton Control instead.

Creates a set of push buttons or picture push buttons.

[[C0]]

row, column

 Row and column are numeric expressions with values of 0 or greater that determine where the first button in a set of push buttons appears.

 The first row is number 0 in the main [[T0]] window or a user-defined window. Rows are numbered from top to bottom. In [[T1]] for Windows, row 0 is the row immediately under the [[T2]] system menu bar. In [[T3]] for Macintosh, row 0 is the row immediately under the [[T4]] title bar. In [[T5]] for [[T6]]-[[T7]], row 0 is the row the [[T8]] system menu bar occupies. See [[T9]] for information about manipulating the system menu bar so you can place output on row 0 in [[T10]] for [[T11]]-[[T12]].

 The first column is number 0 in the main [[T13]] window or a user-defined window. Columns are numbered from left to right.

 When the first button in a set of push buttons is directed to a user-defined window, the row and column coordinates are relative to the user-defined window, not the main [[T14]] window.

 In [[T15]] for Windows and [[T16]] for Macintosh, a position in the main [[T17]] window or in a user-defined window is determined by the font of the main [[T18]] window or the user-defined window. Most fonts can be displayed in a wide variety of sizes, and some are proportionally spaced. A row corresponds to the height of the current font; a column corresponds to the average width of a letter in the current font.

In [[T0]] for Windows and [[T1]] for Macintosh, you can position the first button in a set of push buttons in a window with decimal fractions for row and column coordinates. In [[T2]] for [[T3]]-[[T4]], decimal fractions used for row and column coordinates are rounded to the nearest integer value.

 memvar | field

 When you choose a push button, your choice is stored to the memory variable or array element memvar or to the field field. memvar or field must be of numeric or character type.

 If memvar or field is of numeric type, a number corresponding to the push button choice is stored to the memory variable, array element or field specified with memvar or field. For example, if you create four push buttons and choose the third button, 3 is stored. If memvar or field is of character type, the prompt of the push button you choose is stored to the memory variable, array element or field specified with memvar or field.

 [[T5]] [[T6]] | [[T7]] [[T8]]

 When creating push buttons, you must include the [[T9]] clause, the [[T10]] clause or both. There is no advantage to any of the three methods. The [[T11]] or [[T12]] clause contains the push button specification code, an asterisk (*), and the text for the individual push button prompts.

The [[T0]] character expression [[T1]] must begin with *. To create the push button prompts, include a space after the asterisk followed by a list of the prompts separated by semicolons. One button is created for each prompt. For example, the following [[T2]] clause creates push buttons with the prompts [[T3]] and Cancel:

 ... [[T4]] '* [[T5]];Cancel' [[T6]] 1, 8 ...

 The [[T7]] character expression [[T8]] uses the same syntax as the [[T9]] character expression except the [[T10]] character expression must begin with @ followed by an asterisk (*). For example, the following [[T11]] clause creates push buttons with the prompts [[T12]] and Cancel:

 .. [[T13]] '@* [[T14]];Cancel' [[T15]] 1, 8 ...

 You can also include both the [[T16]] and [[T17]] clauses to create push buttons. If both are included, the [[T18]] character expression [[T19]] must contain * to create the push buttons followed by a space and the push button prompts. The [[T20]] character expression [[T21]] can include prompts to create additional push buttons.

 The following examples illustrate the various forms of syntax you can use to create push buttons. Two push buttons are created: [[T22]] and Cancel. The first button ([[T23]]) is placed in the second row and second column. A number corresponding to the button chosen is stored to the memory variable [[T24]].

 [[T25]] clause only:

 [[T26]] 1 [[T27]] mchoice

@ 2,2 [[T0]] mchoice [[T1]] '* [[T2]];Cancel' [[T3]] 1, 8

 [[T4]] 1 [[T5]] mchoice

 [[T6]] '* [[T7]];Cancel' [[T8]] mprompts

 @ 2,2 [[T9]] mchoice [[T10]] mprompts [[T11]] 1, 8

 [[T12]] clause only:

 [[T13]] 1 [[T14]] mchoice

 @ 2,2 [[T15]] mchoice [[T16]] '@* [[T17]];Cancel' [[T18]] 1, 8

 [[T19]] 1 [[T20]] mchoice

 @ 2,2 [[T21]] mchoice [[T22]] '@*' + ' [[T23]];Cancel' [[T24]] 1, 8

 [[T25]] and [[T26]] clauses:

 [[T27]] 1 [[T28]] mchoice

 @ 2,2 [[T29]] mchoice [[T30]] '*' ;

 [[T31]] ' [[T32]];Cancel' [[T33]] 1, 8

 [[T34]]

 Push Buttons with Picture Prompts

 In [[T35]] for Windows and [[T36]] for Macintosh, the prompt for a push button can also be the name of a picture file. In [[T37]] for Windows, the picture file can be a bitmap file with a .[[T38]] extension. In [[T39]] for Macintosh, you can use a picture file of [[T40]] type or a .[[T41]] bitmap file.

 When a push button uses a picture file for a prompt, the push button mimics the behavior of a push button with a text prompt. For example, the picture file appears on a button but the push button isn't displayed. Like choosing a push button, choosing the picture prompt stores the push button's value to memvar or field.

To use a picture file in a push button, add B to the push button specification code. The [[T0]] and [[T1]] clause specification codes that create a push button are * and @*, respectively. To create a push button with picture prompts, use the codes *B and @*B, followed by a space and the picture filename. If the picture file is not located in the default directory or folder, include the path to the picture file with the picture filename.

 -------------------------------

 Note - The pictures aren't clipped, reduced or enlarged to fit the push button. Use the [[T2]] clause to adjust the size of the push buttons to accommodate the pictures.

 -------------------------------

 If you omit the extension for the picture file, [[T3]] for Macintosh first looks for a picture file with the name you specified and a .[[T4]] extension. If a picture file with a .[[T5]] extension and the name you specified isn't found, [[T6]] for Macintosh then looks for a file with the name you specified and a .[[T7]] extension. If a picture file with a .[[T8]] extension and the name you specified isn't found, [[T9]] for Macintosh then looks for a picture file with the name you specified without an extension.

 Picture Masks and Push Buttons

In [[T0]] for Windows and [[T1]] for Macintosh, a picture push button has three states: up, down and disabled. [[T2]] automatically controls the appearance of a picture push button when it is in each of these three states, but you can override the default appearance by using a picture mask.

 A mask is used to control the transparent areas of a picture push button. By default, the white areas are transparent. If a mask is present, the white areas of the mask, not the picture file, are transparent.

 A mask is a monochrome picture file. In [[T3]] for Windows, a mask is a .[[T4]] with an .[[T5]] extension. In [[T6]] for Macintosh, a mask can be a .[[T7]] with an .[[T8]] extension or a [[T9]] type file with a .[[T10]] extension. The mask must have the same base name as the picture file and the appropriate extension. [[T11]] automatically looks for a mask for a picture file in the same directory or folder where the picture file is located.

 In most cases, a mask isn't necessary. If you don't need anything in your picture to appear white or your picture file has a white background, the picture push button will appear as desired in the up, down and disabled states.

When a picture push button has a mask and is in the up or down state, any white areas in the picture file appear transparent, allowing the color of the button face to show through. However, you can maintain the white color of certain areas.

 Suppose that you have a picture file with a dog on a white background; the dog has white eyes and the button face is red. You want the background of the button to appear red but you want the dog's eyes to be white, not red. Make a mask that is the same size as the picture file but includes only two colors, black and white. Leave the background of the mask white but make the dog - including his eyes - completely black. When the button appears, the background is red to match the button face but the dog's eyes are white.

 When a picture push button is disabled, any white areas in the picture file appear transparent so the color of the button face shows through. Any non-white areas appear dark gray. If the button has a mask, all white areas in the mask are transparent so the color of the button face shows through, and all black areas appear dark gray.

 [[T0]] and [[T1]] Options N, T, H, V, 2 and 3

 Additional options can be combined with the * specification code to modify the behavior (N and T) and appearance (H, V, 2 and 3) of push buttons.
textos.2b5b18e4-b902-4d8a-8cb7-4eef9f3a60a3#315:
The 2 (two-dimensional) and 3 (three-dimensional) specification codes are only available in [[T0]] for Macintosh.

 Option Description

 ------ -----------

 N Does not terminate the [[T1]] when a push button is chosen.

 T Terminates the [[T2]] when a push button is chosen. This is the default behavior.

 H Position the push buttons in a horizontal row.

 V Position the push buttons in a vertical column. This is the default orientation.

 2 Creates flat (two-dimensional) black-and-white push buttons identical to push buttons in Macintosh dialogs.

 3 Creates three-dimensional push buttons identical to push buttons in [[T3]] for Macintosh dialogs. This is the default push button type in [[T4]] for Macintosh.

 You can combine the T or N option with the H, V and 2 or 3 options. For example, the following clause creates a horizontal row of buttons and doesn't cause the [[T5]] to terminate when one of the buttons is chosen:

 ... [[T6]] '*[[T7]] ... '

 In [[T8]] for Macintosh, the following clause creates a horizontal row of two-dimensional buttons and doesn't cause the [[T9]] to terminate when one of the buttons is chosen:

 ... [[T10]] '*[[T11]] ... '

 Push Buttons with Special Features

You can assign a hot key to a button, disable a button, or create a default or escape button. To assign these special features to a push button, you must include special characters when defining the prompt. The special characters are removed when the prompt is stored to memvar or field.

 Hot Keys

 In [[T0]] for [[T1]]-[[T2]], a hot key is a highlighted letter in the push button prompt that you can type to immediately choose a push button. Pressing the hot key selects the button and chooses it. To assign a hot key, place a backslash and a less-than sign (\<) before the desired character of the push button prompt.

 A hot key doesn't choose the push button if the current object is a [[T3]] field, a text-editing region, a pop-up or a list.

 If the current object is an @ ... [[T4]] input field or a text-editing region, pressing the hot key enters the character in the field or the text-editing region. If the current object is a popup or a list, pressing the hot key selects the first option on the popup or list whose prompt begins with the hot key character.

 In [[T5]] for Windows, a hot key is an underlined letter in the push button prompt that you can type to immediately choose the button. If the current object is an @ ... [[T6]] input field, a text-editing region, a popup or a list and [[T7]] is set to [[T8]], you can press the Alt key and the hot key to choose the push button.
